Except in cases when the state of New York, or any of its agencies or municipal corporations is the judgment creditor, or if the debt enforced is for child support, spousal support, maintenance or alimony, provided that in those instances the execution contains a legend at the top thereof, above the caption, in sixteen point bold type with the following language: “The judgment creditor is the state of New York, or any of its agencies or municipal corporations, AND/OR the debt enforced is for child support, spousal support, maintenance or alimony.”, an execution notice shall state that, pursuant to subdivision (l) of section fifty-two hundred five of this article, two thousand five hundred dollars of an account containing direct deposit or electronic payments reasonably identifiable as statutorily exempt payments, as defined in paragraph two of subdivision (l) of section fifty-two hundred five of this article, is exempt from execution and that the garnishee cannot levy upon or restrain two thousand five hundred dollars in such an account. Except in cases when the state of New York, or any of its agencies or municipal corporations is the judgment creditor, or if the debt enforced is for child support, spousal support, maintenance or alimony, provided that in those instances the execution contains a legend at the top thereof, above the caption, in sixteen point bold type with the following language: “The judgment creditor is the state of New York, or any of its agencies or municipal corporations, AND/OR the debt enforced is for child support, spousal support, maintenance or alimony.”, an execution notice shall likewise state that pursuant to subdivision (i) of section fifty-two hundred twenty-two of this article, an execution shall not apply to an amount equal to or less than ninety percent of the greater of two hundred forty times the federal minimum hourly wage prescribed in the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 or two hundred forty times the state minimum hourly wage prescribed in section six hundred fifty-two of the labor law as in effect at the time the earnings are payable, except such part as a court determines to be unnecessary for the reasonable requirements of the judgment debtor and his or her dependents. Where the judgment or order was entered in a court other than the supreme, county or a family court, the execution shall also specify the date on which a transcript of the judgment or order was filed with the clerk of the county in which the judgment was entered. Where jurisdiction in the action was based upon a levy upon property or debt pursuant to an order of attachment, the execution shall also state that fact, describe all property and debts levied upon, and direct that only such property and debts be sold thereunder. Where the judgment or order was recovered for all or part of a mortgage debt, the execution shall also describe the mortgaged property, specify the book and page where the mortgage is recorded, and direct that no part of the mortgaged property be levied upon or sold thereunder. (b) Issuance. At any time before a judgment or order is satisfied or vacated, an execution may be issued from the supreme court, county court or a family court, in the county in which the judgment was first docketed, by the clerk of the court or the attorney for the judgment creditor as officer of the court, to the sheriffs of one or more counties of the state, directing each of them to satisfy the judgment or order out of the real and personal property of the judgment debtor or obligor and the debts due to him or her. Provided, however, if the applicable interest rate changes pursuant to section five thousand four of this chapter while an execution is ongoing, the clerk of the court of the supreme court, county court or a family court, in the county in which the judgment was first docketed, or the attorney for the judgment creditor as officer of the court, shall be authorized to issue an amended execution to the sheriffs of one or more counties of the state and shall issue an amended execution within sixty days of the effective date of the chapter of the laws of two thousand twenty-one which amended this subdivision, effective as of the date of the rate change. Where the judgment or order is for support and is payable to the support collection unit designated by the appropriate social services district, such unit shall be authorized to issue the execution and to satisfy the judgment or order out of the real and personal property of the judgment debtor or obligor and the debts due to him or her. (c) Return. An execution shall be returned to the clerk of the court from which it was issued or to the support collection unit within sixty days after issuance unless the execution has been served in accordance with section 5231 or subdivision (a) of section 5232. The time may be extended in writing for a period of not more than sixty additional days by the attorney for the judgment creditor or by the support collection unit. Further like extensions may be given by the attorney for the judgment creditor or by the support collection unit unless another execution against the same judgment debtor or obligor has been delivered to the same enforcement officer and has not been returned.

reason: The enforcement-limits rule states the bank exemption; 5232 adds the levy's 90-day life, the 4-day notice to a natural-person debtor, the 27-day bank hold with exemption forms, and the creditor's liability for naming a third party's property.

proposed.instrument: NY Civil Practice Law and Rules
proposed.condition: The landlord levies on a natural-person former tenant's bank account or other personal property under an execution.
proposed.effect: The levy is made by serving the execution on the garnishee (bank, employer, other holder), or by seizure of property capable of delivery. It binds property and debts then held or later coming due until transferred to the enforcement officer, and is void 90 days after service except as to what was transferred or is in a CPLR 5225/5227 turnover proceeding, unless the court extends it on the creditor's motion. The officer mails or delivers to the tenant, within four days after serving a garnishee, the execution with the CPLR 5222(e) exemption notice unless it was served within the prior year, to the residence, else in a 'personal and confidential' envelope to the workplace, else any known address. On a bank account: $2,500 is untouchable where identifiable exempt payments were deposited in the prior 45 days, plus the minimum-wage-based amount; the exemption notice and two claim forms are served with the execution; the bank holds the funds at least 27 days and may transfer after 30 days if no claim form or order arrives; no bank fee where the account holds only exempt funds. A creditor that names in its notice property or a debt belonging to someone other than the tenant is liable to that person for damages from the levy.
proposed.quote: (a) Levy by service of execution. The sheriff or support collection unit designated by the appropriate social services district shall levy upon any interest of the judgment debtor or obligor in personal property not capable of delivery, or upon any debt owed to the judgment debtor or obligor, by serving a copy of the execution upon the garnishee, in the same manner as a summons, except that such service shall not be made by delivery to a person authorized to receive service of summons solely by a designation filed pursuant to a provision of law other than rule 318. In the event the garnishee is the state of New York, such levy shall be made in the same manner as an income execution pursuant to section 5231 of this article. A levy by service of the execution is effective only if, at the time of service, the person served owes a debt to the judgment debtor or obligor or he or she is in the possession or custody of property not capable of delivery in which he or she knows or has reason to believe the judgment debtor or obligor has an interest, or if the judgment creditor or support collection unit has stated in a notice which shall be served with the execution that a specified debt is owed by the person served to the judgment debtor or obligor or that the judgment debtor or obligor has an interest in specified property not capable of delivery in the possession or custody of the person served. All property not capable of delivery in which the judgment debtor or obligor is known or believed to have an interest then in or thereafter coming into the possession or custody of such a person, including any specified in the notice, and all debts of such a person, including any specified in the notice, then due or thereafter coming due to the judgment debtor or obligor, shall be subject to the levy. The person served with the execution shall forthwith transfer all such property, and pay all such debts upon maturity, to the sheriff or to the support collection unit and execute any document necessary to effect the transfer or payment. After such transfer or payment, property coming into the possession or custody of the garnishee, or debt incurred by him, or her shall not be subject to the levy. Until such transfer or payment is made, or until the expiration of ninety days after the service of the execution upon him or her, or of such further time as is provided by any order of the court served upon him or her, whichever event first occurs, the garnishee is forbidden to make or suffer any sale, assignment or transfer of, or any interference with, any such property, or pay over or otherwise dispose of any such debt, to any person other than the sheriff or the support collection unit, except upon direction of the sheriff or the support collection unit or pursuant to an order of the court. At the expiration of ninety days after a levy is made by service of the execution, or of such further time as the court, upon motion of the judgment creditor or support collection unit has provided, the levy shall be void except as to property or debts which have been transferred or paid to the sheriff or to the support collection unit or as to which a proceeding under sections 5225 or 5227 has been brought. A judgment creditor who, or support collection unit which, has specified personal property or debt to be levied upon in a notice served with an execution shall be liable to the owner of the property or the person to whom the debt is owed, if other than the judgment debtor or obligor, for any damages sustained by reason of the levy. (b) Levy by seizure. The sheriff or support collection unit of the appropriate social services district shall levy upon any interest of the judgment debtor in personal property capable of delivery by taking the property into custody without interfering with the lawful possession of pledgees and lessees. The sheriff or support collection unit shall forthwith serve a copy of the execution in the manner prescribed by subdivision (a) upon the person from whose possession or custody the property was taken. (c) Notice to judgment debtor or obligor. Where an execution does not state that a notice in the form presented by subdivision (e) of section fifty-two hundred twenty-two of this chapter has been duly served upon the judgment debtor or obligor within a year, the sheriff or support collection unit shall, not later than four days after service of the execution upon any garnishee, mail by first class mail, or personally deliver, to each judgment debtor or obligor who is a natural person, a copy of the execution together with such notice. The sheriff or support collection unit shall specify on the notice to judgment debtor or obligor the name and address of the judgment creditor or the judgment creditor’s attorney or the support collection unit. The notice shall be mailed to the judgment debtor or obligor at his or her residence address; and in the event such mailing is returned as undeliverable by the post office, or if the residence address of the judgment debtor or obligor is unknown, then to the judgment debtor or obligor in care of the place of employment of the judgment debtor or obligor if known, in an envelope bearing the legend “personal and confidential” and not indicating on the outside thereof, by the return address or otherwise, that the communication is from a sheriff or support collection unit or concerns a debt; or if neither the residence nor the place of employment of the judgment debtor or obligor is known, then to the judgment debtor or obligor at any other known address. (d) For the purposes of this section “obligor” shall mean an individual other than a judgment debtor obligated to pay support, alimony or maintenance pursuant to an order of a court of competent jurisdiction who has been found to be in “default” of such order as such term is defined in paragraph seven of subdivision (a) of section fifty-two hundred forty-one of this article and the establishment of such default has been subject to the procedures established for the determination of a “mistake of fact” for income executions pursuant to subdivision (e) of section fifty-two hundred forty-one of this article, except that for the purposes of this section only, a default shall not be founded upon retroactive child support obligations as defined in paragraph (c) of subdivision one of section four hundred forty and subdivision one of section two hundred forty, and paragraph b of subdivision nine of section two hundred thirty-six of the domestic relations law. (e) Notwithstanding the provisions of subdivision (a) of this section, if direct deposit or electronic payments reasonably identifiable as statutorily exempt payments as defined in paragraph two of subdivision (l) of section fifty-two hundred five of this article were made to the judgment debtor’s account during the forty-five day period preceding the date that the execution notice was served on the garnishee banking institution, then a garnishee banking institution shall not execute, levy, attach, garnish or otherwise restrain or encumber two thousand five hundred dollars in the judgment debtor’s account. Notwithstanding the provisions of subdivision (a) of this section, an execution shall not apply to an amount equal to or less than the greater of two hundred forty times the federal minimum hourly wage prescribed in the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 or two hundred forty times the state minimum hourly wage prescribed in section six hundred fifty-two of the labor law as in effect at the time the earnings are payable (as published on the websites of the United States department of labor and the state department of labor) except such part thereof as a court determines to be unnecessary for the reasonable requirements of the judgment debtor and his or her dependents. This amount shall be equal to seventeen hundred sixteen dollars on the effective date of this subdivision, and shall rise to seventeen hundred forty dollars on July twenty-fourth, two thousand nine, and shall rise thereafter in tandem with the minimum wage. Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to limit a banking institution’s right or obligation to restrain, remove or execute upon such funds from the judgment debtor’s account if required by 42 U.S.C. § 659 or 38 U.S.C. § 5301 or to enforce a child support, spousal support, alimony or maintenance obligation or by a court order. Nothing in this subdivision shall alter the exempt status of funds that are protected from execution, levy, attachment, garnishment, or other legal process, under section fifty-two hundred five of this article or under any other provision of state or federal law, or affect the right of a judgment debtor to claim such exemption. (f) Fee for banking institution’s costs in processing a levy by service of execution when account contains only exempt, direct deposit or electronic payments. In the event that a banking institution cannot lawfully garnish or execute upon on a judgment debtor’s banking institution account or funds are garnished or executed upon in violation of any section of this chapter, the banking institution shall charge no fee to the judgment debtor regardless of any terms of agreement, or schedule of fees, or other contract between the judgment debtor and the banking institution.

reason: Says who drafts the judgment document (the winner's attorney or the clerk, the loser after 30 days); it changes no amount, deadline or step in settling or collecting the account.

The 3215 rules state the default mailing and limitations affidavit; no rule states that in NYC Civil Court a default judgment may be entered on a summons endorsed with the amount and the nature of the claim, without a formal complaint.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord sues a former tenant for the balance in NYC Civil Court and the tenant does not appear or answer.
proposed.effect: A default judgment is entered under CPLR 3215. A summons that states the amount for which the landlord will take judgment on default and the nature and substance of the claim, or a summons served with a formal complaint, counts as the summons and complaint for CPLR 3215(e) proof. The 3215(g)(3) additional mailing, the limitations affidavit and the military affidavit still apply (NY:CPLR-3215(g)(3), NY:CPLR-3215(j)-sol-affidavit, US:50USC3931(b)(1)).
proposed.quote: A judgment by default may be entered as provided in CPLR § 3215. A summons stating the amount for which the plaintiff will take judgment if the defendant fails to appear and answer, and containing a statement of the nature and substance of the cause of action, or a summons accompanied by a formal complaint, shall be deemed "the summons and the complaints" referred to in subdivision (e) of said section.

reason: Makes a former tenant's confession of judgment (CPLR 3218) enterable and enforceable in NYC Civil Court for a balance within its jurisdiction; a settlement and payment-plan option.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A former tenant signs an affidavit confessing judgment for a balance within the NYC Civil Court's monetary jurisdiction (the affidavit's requisites and filing limits: NY:CPLR-3218-confession).
proposed.effect: The affidavit is filed with the Civil Court clerk in the county (in place of the county clerk named in CPLR 3218(b)); the judgment is entered in the Civil Court and enforced like any Civil Court judgment.
proposed.quote: The provisions of CPLR § 3218, relating to judgment by confession, shall be applicable in this court where the relief for which the judgment is confessed is within the jurisdiction of this court. For such purpose the words "clerk of the county" as used in CPLR § 3218 (b) shall be deemed a reference to the clerk of this court in such county, and such judgment shall be entered in this court and shall be enforcible in the same manner and with the same effect as a judgment in an action in this court.

reason: Says who issues an execution on an NYC Civil Court judgment (the creditor's attorney, or the clerk if the creditor has no attorney) and that Supreme Court time limits apply; changes how a self-represented owner enforces.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord enforces an NYC Civil Court money judgment (or an order directing payment of money) against a former tenant.
proposed.effect: The execution, including an income execution, is issued by the landlord's attorney or, if the landlord has no attorney (an individual owner in small claims), by the clerk of the court in the county where the judgment was entered, within the time allowed in the Supreme Court (at any time before satisfaction: NY:CPLR-5230-execution).
proposed.quote: An execution, including an income execution, upon a judgment may be issued by the judgment-creditor's attorney or, if he does not appear by attorney, by the clerk of the court in the county where the judgment was entered. It shall be issued within the time prescribed by law applicable in the supreme court. A "judgment", as used in this article, shall be deemed to include an order directing the payment of money.

reason: To reach real property, or to enforce through county clerks and sheriffs outside the city, the landlord must obtain the Civil Court transcript and docket it with the county clerk; this decides where a moved-away tenant can be pursued.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord holds an NYC Civil Court judgment against a former tenant and wants to docket it with a county clerk (to create a lien on the tenant's real property or to enforce outside New York City).
proposed.effect: On the landlord's application the clerk delivers a transcript of the judgment; docketing with the county clerk and then with other county clerks follows the CPLR (CPLR 5018). Only a docketed judgment reaches real property (NY:CCA-1505-real-property).
proposed.quote: (a) Upon application of a judgment-creditor the clerk must deliver to him a transcript of the judgment. If the judgment is for other than money only, the clerk shall insert in the transcript a brief statement of the nature of the action and the relief awarded by the judgment; such statement may be inserted under "remarks" as contained in the form set forth in § 255-c of the judiciary law. (b) The docketing of the judgment with the clerk of the county, and thereafter with other county clerks, shall be governed by the CPLR.

reason: An NYC Civil Court execution reaches only the tenant's personal property, goes to a city marshal or the city sheriff, and may be levied anywhere in the city without docketing; this sets the reach of enforcement.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord issues an execution out of the NYC Civil Court on a judgment against a former tenant.
proposed.effect: It may be levied only on the tenant's personal property (bank accounts, wages by income execution, other personal property), is directed to a city marshal or the New York City sheriff (delivered to the sheriff's office in the county of levy), is signed by the clerk of the county where judgment was entered or by the creditor's attorney, bears its delivery date and the CPLR 5230 contents, and may be levied anywhere in New York City without docketing the judgment with a county clerk. Property outside the city, or real property, requires a transcript docketed with the county clerk (NY:CCA-1502-transcript, NY:CCA-1505-real-property).
proposed.quote: An execution issued out of this court may be levied only against personal property of the judgment-debtor. It shall be directed either to a marshal or the sheriff of the city of New York, and if directed to the sheriff it must be delivered to the office of the sheriff in the county in which it is to be levied. It must be subscribed by either the clerk of the court in the county in which the judgment was entered, or the attorney for the judgment-creditor, and must bear, in addition to such other matter as is required by the CPLR, the date of its delivery. It may be levied in any part of the city of New York, and for such purpose it is not necessary that the judgment have been docketed with any county clerk.

reason: A Civil Court execution cannot reach real property; a transcript must be filed with the county clerk first, after which the judgment is a lien and enforceable against real property.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord holds an NYC Civil Court judgment against a former tenant who owns real property.
proposed.effect: No execution out of the Civil Court may be levied on real property. The landlord first files a transcript with the county clerk of the county where judgment was entered (NY:CCA-1502-transcript); CPLR 5018(a) then applies and the judgment is enforced against real property accordingly (subject to the homestead exemption, CPLR 5206). A Civil Court execution against personal property may still issue after transcripting.
proposed.quote: An execution out of this court may not be levied against real property. In order for an execution on a judgment of this court to be levied against real property, a transcript of such judgment must be filed with the county clerk of the county wherein judgment was entered, pursuant to § 1502 of this act After such transcripting, CPLR § 5018 (a) shall be applicable and the judgment enforceable accordingly. This shall not be construed to prevent the issuance of an execution out of this court, pursuant and subject to § 1504 of this act, after such transcripting.

reason: Where the tenant's real property was attached before judgment, execution must issue out of Supreme Court after docketing; changes the enforcement route in that case.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord obtained an order of attachment levied on the former tenant's real property that has not been vacated, and then an NYC Civil Court judgment.
proposed.effect: Execution may not issue out of the Civil Court; the landlord files and dockets a transcript with the county clerk and the execution issues out of the Supreme Court.
proposed.quote: Where the real property of the judgment-debtor has been duly attached under an order of attachment that has not been vacated, the execution may not issue out of this court. In such a case, a transcript of the judgment must be filed and docketed with the county clerk and the execution issued out of supreme court.

reason: Lets the NYC Civil Court grant injunctions, restraining notices and receivers in an enforcement proceeding within CPLR 5221, with statewide service; an enforcement option against a tenant who moved away.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord enforces an NYC Civil Court money judgment in an enforcement proceeding of which the Civil Court has jurisdiction under CPLR 5221.
proposed.effect: The court may issue an injunction, restraining order or restraining notice and appoint a receiver in furtherance of enforcing the money judgment; its papers may be served anywhere, regardless of city or state lines, as in the Supreme Court, and a receiver's powers extend throughout the state.
proposed.quote: (a) An injunction or restraining order or notice may issue out of or by, and a receiver may be appointed by, the court if: 1. the court has been granted jurisdiction of an enforcement proceeding by CPLR § 5221; and 2. such remedy is utilized in furtherance of the enforcement of a money judgment. (b) In any enforcement proceeding of which the court has jurisdiction, all processes, mandates, subpoenas, orders, notices and other papers therein may be served or executed by such means and at such place, regardless of city or state lines, as would be authorized in the supreme court in a like instance; and the powers of a receiver appointed in such proceeding, pursuant to subdivision (a), shall extend throughout the state.

reason: In small claims an itemized paid invoice, or two itemized estimates, is prima facie proof of the reasonable value and necessity of repairs; this sets how the landlord proves a damage charge (or the tenant disproves it) and what the settlement file must hold.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A claim between the landlord and a former tenant (a tenant's deposit claim, or an individual owner's damage claim) is heard in the NYC small claims part.
proposed.effect: The court decides to do substantial justice under the substantive law and is not bound by rules of practice, pleading or evidence, except privilege and the dead-man rule. An itemized bill or invoice, receipted or marked paid, or two itemized estimates for services or repairs, are admissible and are prima facie evidence of the reasonable value and necessity of the work; the landlord keeps the burden of proving the amount kept was reasonable (NY:GOL-7-108(1-a)(f)). Disclosure is available only by court order on proper circumstances. Where the claim arises from the defendant's business, the judge identifies its licensing authority and business associations. Operator step: for each damage charge keep the itemized paid invoice, or two itemized estimates where the work is not yet done (NY:CASE-Toporek-estimate).
proposed.quote: The court shall conduct hearings upon small claims in such manner as to do substantial justice between the parties according to the rules of substantive law and shall not be bound by statutory provisions or rules of practice, procedure, pleading or evidence, except statutory provisions relating to privileged communications and personal transactions or communications with a decedent or person with a mental illness. An itemized bill or invoice, receipted or marked paid, or two itemized estimates for services or repairs, are admissible in evidence and are prima facie evidence of the reasonable value and necessity of such services and repairs. Disclosure shall be unavailable in small claims procedure except upon order of the court on showing of proper circumstances. In every small claims action, where the claim arises out of the conduct of the defendant's business at the hearing on the matter, the judge or arbitrator shall determine the appropriate state or local licensing or certifying authority and any business or professional association of which the defendant is a member. The provisions of this act and the rules of this court, together with the statutes and rules governing supreme court practice, shall apply to claims brought under this article so far as the same can be made applicable and are not in conflict with the provisions of this article; in case of conflict, the provisions of this article shall control.

reason: Small-claims remedies: conditional judgments, pre-judgment examination and restraint of the defendant, transfer, and a bar on counterclaims beyond the small-claims limit; changes whether a landlord sued for the deposit can counterclaim the balance there.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A small claim between the landlord and a former tenant is decided in the NYC small claims part.
proposed.effect: The court directs judgment on its findings and may condition its entry on just terms; before judgment it may order the defendant examined and restrain it as if a post-judgment restraining notice had been served (CPLR 5229). It may transfer the claim to another part. A counterclaim is allowed only if it is within the small-claims monetary limit ($10,000); a landlord sued for the deposit whose balance claim exceeds the limit brings that claim in a court of competent jurisdiction instead. If the defendant appears to act fraudulently or illegally in a licensed business (for example a licensed broker-manager), the court advises the licensing authority or tells the claimant to, and keeps the case.
proposed.quote: (a) Upon determination of a small claim, the court shall direct judgment in accordance with its findings, and, when necessary to do substantial justice between the parties, may condition the entry of judgment upon such terms as the court shall deem proper. Pursuant to section fifty-two hundred twenty-nine of the civil practice law and rules, prior to entering a judgment, the court may order the examination of or disclosure by, the defendant and restrain him to the same extent as if a restraining notice had been served upon him after judgment was entered. (b) The court shall have power to transfer any small claim or claims to any other part of the court upon such terms as the rules may provide, and proceed to hear the same according to the usual practice and procedure applicable to other parts of the court. (c) No counterclaim shall be permitted in a small claims action, unless the court would have had monetary jurisdiction over the counterclaim if it had been filed as a small claim. Any other claim sought to be maintained against the claimant may be filed in any court of competent jurisdiction. (d) If the defendant appears to be engaged in repeated fraudulent or illegal acts or otherwise demonstrates persistent fraud or illegality in the carrying on, conducting or transaction of business, the court shall either advise the attorney general in relation to his authority under subdivision twelve of section sixty-three of the executive law, or shall advise the claimant to do same, but shall retain jurisdiction over the small claim.

reason: A landlord sued in small claims may move the case to a jury part by demand, fee, affidavit and a $50 undertaking; the claimant waives a jury and may get up to $25 costs after transfer.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A former tenant brings a small claim against the landlord (or an individual owner brings one against the tenant).
proposed.effect: The claimant waives a jury unless the case is removed to a regular part. The defendant may, before the day it must appear, file a jury demand with an affidavit specifying the issues of fact and stating good faith, the jury fee, and a $50 undertaking (or $50 cash) securing costs payable within 30 days of entry; the case is then transferred and may require pleadings. If a transferred claim succeeds, the court may award the claimant costs up to $25.
proposed.quote: A person commencing an action upon a small claim under this article shall be deemed to have waived a trial by jury, but if said action shall be removed to a regular part of the court, the plaintiff shall have the same right to demand a trial by jury as if such action had originally been begun in such part. Any party to such action, other than the plaintiff, prior to the day upon which he is notified to appear or answer, may file with the court a demand for a trial by jury and his affidavit that there are issues of fact in the action requiring such a trial, specifying the same and stating that such trial is desired and intended in good faith. Such demand and affidavit shall be accompanied with the jury fee required by law and an undertaking in the sum of fifty dollars in such form as may be approved by the rules, payable to the other party or parties, conditioned upon the payment of any costs which may be entered against him in the said action or any appeal within thirty days after the entry thereof; or, in lieu of said undertaking, the sum of fifty dollars may be deposited with the clerk of the court and thereupon the clerk shall forthwith transmit such original papers or duly attested copies thereof as may be provided by the rules to the part of the court to which the action shall have been transferred and assigned and such part may require pleadings in such action as though it had been begun by the service of a summons. Such action may be considered a preferred cause of action. In any small claim which may have been transferred to another part of the court, the court may award costs up to twenty-five dollars to the plaintiff if he prevails.

reason: The commercial-claims counterpart: the former tenant sued in the commercial claims part may demand a jury with fee, affidavit and $50 undertaking; the owner may get up to $25 costs after transfer.

Such action may be considered a preferred cause of action. In any commercial claim which may have been transferred to another part of the court, the court may award costs up to twenty-five dollars to the claimant if the claimant prevails.

reason: Limits appeal from a small-claims judgment to substantial-justice review; appellate practice, which changes no settlement or collection step.

In the commercial claims part the clerk mails notice of a default judgment and the defaulting tenant may seek vacatur in writing with a reasonable excuse under CPLR 5015; changes whether a default judgment on the balance holds. The appeal limit in (a) is appellate practice.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: An entity owner obtains a default judgment against a former tenant in the commercial claims part.
proposed.effect: The clerk mails notice of the default judgment by first-class mail to both parties, telling the tenant of its obligation to pay, that non-payment may lead to garnishment and seizure, and that with a reasonable excuse it may apply in writing to vacate the default. Proceedings on default follow CPLR 5015 (NY:CPLR-5015-relief-from-judgment).
proposed.quote: (b) The clerk shall mail notice of the default judgment by first class mail, both to the claimant and to the party complained against. Such notice shall inform the defaulting party, in language promulgated by the state office of court administration, of such party's legal obligation to pay; that failure to pay may result in garnishments, repossessions, seizures and similar actions; and that if there was a reasonable excuse for the default, the defaulting party may apply to have the default vacated by submitting a written request to the court. (c) Proceedings on default under this article are to be governed by, but are not limited to, section five thousand fifteen of the civil practice law and rules.

reason: Fixes what a small-claims judgment between landlord and tenant does to later suits: no issue preclusion, claim preclusion as usual, and a later judgment on the same facts reduced by the small-claims award. Decides whether the loser can sue again and what a split claim costs.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A small-claims judgment was entered between the landlord and a former tenant (for example on the tenant's deposit claim, or an individual owner's damage claim), and a party later sues in another action or court over the same tenancy.
proposed.effect: Branch (a) issue preclusion: no fact found in the small-claims judgment binds either party in another action. Branch (b) claim preclusion: the small-claims judgment bars a later claim by the same claimant against the same adversary arising from the same transaction or series of transactions (the tenancy's account), so an owner that sues in small claims for part of the balance cannot later sue for the rest, and a claimant that lost cannot sue again on the same claim (Simmons v Trans Express Inc., 37 NY3d 107 [2021], answering a certified question). Branch (c) set-off: a later judgment in another action involving the same facts, issues and parties is reduced by the small-claims award. Branch (d) the defendant's own claim: a landlord sued in small claims for the deposit that did not counterclaim is not barred from suing later for its balance, because New York has no compulsory counterclaim (CPLR 3019), unless the later claim would impair the rights the small-claims judgment established; the tenant's facts found there do not bind it.
judgment_terms: same transaction or series of transactions
would impair rights established by the prior judgment
proposed.quote: A judgment obtained under this article shall not be deemed an adjudication of any fact at issue or found therein in any other action or court; except that a subsequent judgment obtained in another action or court involving the same facts, issues and parties shall be reduced by the amount of a judgment awarded under this article.

reason: The commercial-claims counterpart of 1808: an entity owner's commercial-claims judgment has no issue preclusion, carries claim preclusion, and reduces a later judgment on the same facts.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A commercial-claims judgment was entered between an entity owner and a former tenant, and a party later sues over the same tenancy.
proposed.effect: No fact found there binds either party in another action; the judgment bars a later claim by the same claimant against the same tenant arising from the same transaction (the tenancy's account), so the owner cannot split its balance between the commercial claims part and a later action (the Court of Appeals' reading of the identical 1808 text in Simmons v Trans Express Inc., 37 NY3d 107 [2021]); a later judgment involving the same facts, issues and parties is reduced by the commercial-claims award. A tenant that did not counterclaim for its deposit may sue for it later unless that would impair the rights the judgment established.
judgment_terms: same transaction or series of transactions
would impair rights established by the prior judgment
proposed.quote: A judgment obtained under this article shall not be deemed an adjudication of any fact at issue or found therein in any other action or court; except that a subsequent judgment obtained in another action or court involving the same facts, issues and parties shall be reduced by the amount of a judgment awarded under this article.

reason: The clerk and court may deny the small claims part to a claimant re-filing a claim already adjudicated or filed to harass; changes whether a losing party can re-file there.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A claimant files a small claim that it previously brought and lost after a hearing, or that the clerk finds is brought to oppress or harass.
proposed.effect: The clerk may require the claimant to apply to the court for leave; if the court finds the claim already adjudicated, or brought solely to oppress or harass and not under color of right, it may deny use of the small claims part for that claim.
judgment_terms: for purposes of oppression or harassment
under color of right
proposed.quote: If the clerk shall find that the procedures of the small claims part are sought to be utilized by a claimant for purposes of oppression or harassment, as where a claimant has previously resorted to such procedures on the same claim and has been unsuccessful after the hearing thereon, the clerk may in his discretion compel the claimant to make application to the court for leave to prosecute the claim in the small claims part. The court upon such application may inquire into the circumstances and, if it shall find that the claim has already been adjudicated, or that the claim is sought to be brought on solely for purposes of oppression or harassment and not under color of right, it may make an order denying the claimant the use of the small claims part to prosecute the claim.

reason: The commercial-claims counterpart of 1810: an owner re-filing an adjudicated or harassing commercial claim may be denied the part.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: An entity owner files a commercial claim against a former tenant that it previously brought and lost after a hearing, or that the clerk finds is brought to oppress or harass.
proposed.effect: The clerk may require the owner to apply for leave; if the court finds the claim already adjudicated, or brought solely to oppress or harass and not under color of right, it may deny use of the commercial claims part for that claim.

The court upon such application may inquire into the circumstances and, if it shall find that the claim has already been adjudicated, or that the claim is sought to be brought on solely for purposes of oppression or harassment and not under color of right, it may make an order denying the claimant the use of the commercial claims part to prosecute the claim.

reason: An unpaid commercial-claims judgment lets the owner get information subpoenas from the clerk at nominal cost with help preparing them; a cost and step in enforcing against the former tenant.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: An entity owner's commercial-claims judgment against a former tenant remains unsatisfied.
proposed.effect: On request the commercial claims clerk issues information subpoenas (CPLR 5224) at nominal cost and helps the owner prepare and use them.
proposed.quote: Where a judgment has been entered in a commercial claims part and remains unsatisfied, the commercial claims clerk shall, upon request, issue information subpoenas, at nominal cost, for the judgment creditor and provide the creditor with assistance on their preparation and use.

reason: A landlord business sued in small claims must pay the judgment in its true name or any business name; one entered under another name and unpaid 35 days after notice lets the tenant sue for the judgment, costs, attorney's fees and $100, and a licensed business risks its licence.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.actor: landlord or managing agent (small-claims judgment debtor)
proposed.condition: A former tenant obtains a small-claims judgment against the landlord, managing agent or other business on a claim arising from its business activities (the deposit, rent paid).
proposed.effect: It must pay the judgment, whether entered in its true name (legal name, or the name under which it is licensed, registered or incorporated) or in any name in which it conducts business (signs, advertising, contracts, invoices, receipts, checks). If entered in a name other than its true name and unpaid 35 days after it receives notice of entry, the tenant may sue in small claims or any court, regardless of the court's monetary limit, for the judgment, costs, reasonable attorney's fees and $100. If the business is licensed (for example a real estate broker managing the building) and the judgment relates to licensed activity, is not stayed or appealed, and is unpaid 35 days after notice, the licensing authority considers a deliberate or patterned failure to pay in revoking, suspending, conditioning or refusing the licence. Treble damages for repeated unpaid judgments: NY:CCA-1812-treble.
proposed.quote: (a) Any person, partnership, firm or corporation which is sued in a small claims court for any cause of action arising out of its business activities, shall pay any judgment rendered against it in its true name or in any name in which it conducts business. "True name" includes the legal name of a natural person and the name under which a partnership, firm or corporation is licensed, registered, incorporated or otherwise authorized to do business. "Conducting business" as used in this section shall include, but not be limited to, maintaining signs at business premises or on business vehicles; advertising; entering into contracts; and printing or using sales slips, checks, invoices or receipts. Whenever a judgment has been rendered against a person, partnership, firm or corporation in other than its true name and the judgment has remained unpaid for thirty-five days after receipt by the judgment debtor of notice of its entry, the aggrieved judgment creditor shall be entitled to commence an action in small claims court or in any other court of otherwise competent jurisdiction against such judgment debtor, notwithstanding the jurisdictional limit of the court, for the sum of the original judgment, costs, reasonable attorney's fees, and one hundred dollars. (b) Whenever a judgment which relates to activities for which a license is required has been rendered against a business which is licensed by a state or local licensing authority and which remains unpaid for thirty-five days after receipt by the judgment debtor of notice of its entry and the judgment has not been stayed or appealed, the state or local licensing authority shall consider such failure to pay if deliberate or part of a pattern of similar conduct indicating recklessness, as a basis for the revocation, suspension, conditioning or refusal to grant or renew such license. Nothing herein shall be construed to preempt an authority's existing policy if it is more restrictive.

reason: The commercial-claims counterpart of 1813: a business judgment debtor in the commercial claims part must pay in any name it uses; a tenant with a counterclaim judgment may sue for the judgment, costs, fees and $100 if unpaid 35 days.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.actor: entity owner (judgment debtor on a counterclaim)
proposed.condition: A former tenant obtains a judgment in the commercial claims part (for example on a deposit counterclaim) against the owner or another business on a claim arising from its business activities.
proposed.effect: It must pay the judgment in its true name or any name in which it conducts business. If entered in another name and unpaid 35 days after notice of entry, the tenant may sue in any competent court, regardless of monetary limit, for the judgment, costs, reasonable attorney's fees and $100; a licensed business's deliberate or patterned non-payment of a judgment on licensed activity counts against its licence.
proposed.quote: (a) Any person, partnership, firm or corporation which is sued in a commercial claims part for any cause of action arising out of its business activities, shall pay any judgment rendered against it in its true name or in any name in which it conducts business. "True name" includes the legal name of a natural person and the name under which a partnership, firm or corporation is licensed, registered, incorporated or otherwise authorized to do business. "Conducting business" as used in this section shall include, but not be limited to, maintaining signs at business premises or on business vehicles; advertising; entering into contracts; and printing or using sales slips, checks, invoices or receipts. Whenever a judgment has been rendered against a person, partnership, firm or corporation in other than its true name and the judgment has remained unpaid for thirty-five days after receipt by the judgment debtor of notice of its entry, the aggrieved judgment creditor shall be entitled to commence an action in commercial claims part or in any other court of otherwise competent jurisdiction against such judgment debtor, notwithstanding the jurisdictional limit of the court, for the sum of the original judgment, costs, reasonable attorney's fees, and one hundred dollars. (b) Whenever a judgment which relates to activities for which a license is required has been rendered against a business which is licensed by a state or local licensing authority and which remains unpaid for thirty-five days after receipt by the judgment debtor of notice of its entry and the judgment has not been stayed or appealed, the state or local licensing authority shall consider such failure to pay if deliberate or part of a pattern of similar conduct indicating recklessness, as a basis for the revocation, suspension, conditioning or refusal to grant or renew such license. Nothing herein shall be construed to preempt an authority's existing policy if it is more restrictive.

reason: A tenant may sue the landlord in small claims under any business name it uses, and a landlord seeking to vacate a small-claims judgment must disclose its true and business names.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A former tenant sues the landlord or managing agent in small claims without knowing its true legal name.
proposed.effect: The tenant may name it by any name it uses in conducting business; the clerk amends the papers when the true name becomes known before the hearing, and the judge determines the true name at the hearing. A landlord that moves under CPLR 5015 to vacate the judgment must disclose its true name and every name it does or did business under at the time of the tenancy.
proposed.quote: (a) A party who is ignorant, in whole or in part, of the true name of a person, partnership, firm or corporation which may properly be made a party defendant, may proceed against such defendant in any name used by the person, partnership, firm or corporation in conducting business, as defined in subdivision (a) of section eighteen hundred thirteen of this article. (b) If the true name of the defendant becomes known at any time prior to the hearing on the merits, such information shall be brought to the attention of the clerk, who shall immediately amend all prior proceedings and papers. The clerk shall send an amended notice to the defendant, without payment of additional fees by the plaintiff, and all subsequent proceedings and papers shall be amended accordingly. (c) In every action in the small claims part, at the hearing on the merits, the judge or arbitrator shall determine the defendant's true name. The clerk shall amend all prior proceedings and papers to conform to such determination, and all subsequent proceedings and papers shall be amended accordingly. (d) A party against whom a judgment has been entered pursuant to this article, in any proceeding under section five thousand fifteen of the civil practice law and rules for relief from such judgment, shall, disclose its true name; any and all names in which it is conducting business; and any and all names in which it was conducting business at the time of the transaction or occurrence on which such judgment is based. All subsequent proceedings and papers shall be amended to conform to such disclosure.

reason: The commercial-claims counterpart of 1814: a business party may be named by its business name, the judge fixes the true name, and a judgment debtor seeking vacatur must disclose its names.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A party to a commercial claim over the tenancy is a business whose true name is unknown to the other side.
proposed.effect: It may be named by any name it uses in business; the clerk amends the papers when the true name is known, the judge determines the true name at the hearing, and a party seeking CPLR 5015 relief from the judgment discloses its true and business names.
proposed.quote: (a) A party who is ignorant, in whole or in part, of the true name of a person, partnership, firm or corporation which may properly be made a party defendant, may proceed against such defendant in any name used by the person, partnership, firm or corporation in conducting business, as defined in subdivision (a) of section eighteen hundred thirteen-A of this article. (b) If the true name of the defendant becomes known at any time prior to the hearing on the merits, such information shall be brought to the attention of the clerk, who shall immediately amend all prior proceedings and papers. The clerk shall send an amended notice to the defendant, without payment of additional fees by the plaintiff, and all subsequent proceedings and papers shall be amended accordingly. (c) In every action in the commercial claims part, at the hearing on the merits, the judge or arbitrator shall determine the defendant's true name. The clerk shall amend all prior proceedings and papers to conform to such determination, and all subsequent proceedings and papers shall be amended accordingly. (d) A party against whom a judgment has been entered pursuant to this article, in any proceeding under section five thousand fifteen of the civil practice law and rules for relief from such judgment, shall disclose its true name; any and all names in which it is conducting business; and any and all names in which it was conducting business at the time of the transaction or occurrence on which such judgment is based. All subsequent proceedings and papers shall be amended to conform to such disclosure.

reason: The appearance rule states who may appear for owners and bars Handoff; 1815 adds that a disabled party (a tenant or an individual owner) may, with leave, appear through an unpaid relative.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.provision: CCA 1815 (first of two sections so numbered)
proposed.condition: A party to an NYC Civil Court case over the tenancy is a natural person who, because of age, mental or physical capacity or other disability, asks that a relative appear for it.
proposed.effect: The court may permit a relative by blood or marriage to appear for that party in the interests of justice. The representative may not charge a fee or accept any remuneration, so Handoff or a paid manager can never appear this way.
proposed.quote: The court may permit, upon the request of a party, that a non-attorney representative, who is related by consanguinity or affinity to such party, be allowed to appear on behalf of such party when the court finds that due to the age, mental or physical capacity or other disability of such party that it is in the interests of justice to permit such representation. No person acting as a non-attorney representative shall be permitted to charge a fee or be allowed to accept any form of remuneration for such services.

reason: Applies CPLR article 85 security for costs in NYC Civil Court with a $200 minimum undertaking; a plaintiff that is not a New York resident or domestic or licensed corporation (a tenant who moved away, a foreign owner) can be made to post security.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: An action between the landlord and a former tenant is in NYC Civil Court and the defendant moves for security for costs (grounds: NY:CPLR-8501-security-for-costs).
proposed.effect: CPLR article 85 applies, except that the minimum undertaking is $200 rather than the CPLR 8503 amount.
proposed.quote: Article 85 of the CPLR, entitled "security for costs", shall apply in this court, except that the minimum undertaking of CPLR 8503 shall be $200 rather than the amount therein provided.

reason: Fixes the costs a prevailing party recovers in an NYC Civil Court action (not small claims or summary proceedings): $50/$100/$150 stages, or $20/$35/$60 when the money judgment is $6,000 or less.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: An action between the landlord and a former tenant ends in judgment in the NYC Civil Court regular or commercial claims part (not small claims, not a summary proceeding).
proposed.effect: Branch (a): money judgment of $6,000 or less: costs are $20 for proceedings before a notice of trial, plus $35 after notice of trial and before trial, plus $60 for each trial, inquest or assessment of damages. Branch (b): any other action: $50, plus $100, plus $150 on the same stages. Disbursements are added (NY:CCA-1908-disbursements). Costs and disbursements are recovered only as the judgment awards them; none goes on the final account before judgment (NY:RPL-234-a).
proposed.quote: (a) Ordinary costs. Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c) of this section, costs awarded in an action shall be in the amount of: 1. fifty dollars for all proceedings before a notice of trial is filed; plus 2. one hundred dollars for all proceedings after a notice of trial is filed and before trial; plus 3. one hundred fifty dollars for each trial, inquest or assessment of damages. (b) Limited costs in certain actions. Costs awarded in an action for a sum of money only where the amount of the judgment is not more than six thousand dollars, shall be in the amount of: 1. twenty dollars for all proceedings before a notice of trial is filed; plus 2. thirty-five dollars for all proceedings after a notice of trial is filed and before trial; plus 3. sixty dollars for each trial, inquest or assessment of damages. (c) This section shall not apply to costs in a summary proceeding or in a small claims actions.

reason: Makes the CPLR rules on who gets costs (8101 prevailing party, 8103 split issues, 8104 consolidated actions, 8105 multiple parties, 8106 motions) apply in NYC Civil Court.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: Costs are decided in an NYC Civil Court action or proceeding between the landlord and a former tenant.
proposed.effect: CPLR 8101 (costs to the party in whose favor judgment is entered), 8103 (separate issues), 8104 (consolidated, severed or removed actions), 8105 (several plaintiffs or defendants) and 8106 (motions) apply.
proposed.quote: The provisions of CPLR §§ 8101, 8103, 8104, 8105 and 8106 shall apply in actions and proceedings in this court.

reason: Adds to Civil Court costs the CPLR 8302/8303(a) allowances and the discretionary allowance on an enforcement motion (8303(b)); changes what a judgment creditor recovers for enforcement motions.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: Costs are computed in an NYC Civil Court action between the landlord and a former tenant, or the landlord moves to enforce a judgment.
proposed.effect: Costs on appeal and those under CCA 1102 are added to ordinary costs. The CPLR 8302 allowance (certain real property actions) and the CPLR 8303(a) discretionary allowance apply and are added on top of ordinary costs. On a motion relating to enforcement of a judgment, the court may award costs under CPLR 8303(b) (NY:CPLR-8303-additional-allowance).
proposed.quote: (a) Certain costs added. Costs on appeal, and those awarded under § 1102 of this act, may be added to the amount of costs otherwise applicable in the action. (b) Additional allowance. 1. Section 8302 of the CPLR, relating to an additional allowance as of right in certain real property actions in which plaintiff has recovered judgment, shall apply in this court. The allowance so calculated shall be added to the amount of costs first calculated under other provisions of this article without reference to CPLR § 8302. 2. Section 8303 (a) of the CPLR, relating to an additional allowance in the court's discretion in certain actions, shall apply in this court to an action within its jurisdiction which falls within CPLR § 8303 (a). The allowance so calculated shall be added to the amount of costs first calculated under other provisions of this article without reference to CPLR § 8303 (a). (c) Discretionary allowance on enforcement motion. Section 8303 (b) of the CPLR, relating to costs on a motion relating to the enforcement of a judgment, shall apply in this court without reference to the foregoing subdivisions of this section.

reason: A former tenant who wins on a bankruptcy-discharge defense recovers no costs; changes the cost exposure of a landlord that sues a discharged tenant.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord sues a former tenant in NYC Civil Court and the tenant wins on the defense of bankruptcy (discharge).
proposed.effect: The tenant is not entitled to costs. The landlord's suit on a discharged balance still violates the discharge injunction (US:11USC524(a)(2)), which carries its own remedies.
proposed.quote: Where the defendant recovers judgment upon the defense of bankruptcy, he shall not be entitled to costs.

reason: The court may impose up to $50 costs on a motion, amendment or trial adjournment; a cost the landlord or tenant may owe or recover in a Civil Court case.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: In an NYC Civil Court case between the landlord and a former tenant, the court grants or denies a motion, allows a pleading amendment or adjourns a trial.
proposed.effect: The court may impose costs of up to $50 in its discretion.
proposed.quote: The court may in its discretion impose costs not exceeding fifty dollars in the following cases: (a) Upon granting or denying a motion. (b) Upon allowing an amendment of a pleading. (c) Upon adjournment of a trial.

reason: The clerk taxes costs and clerk and execution fees into the judgment; other disbursements need two days' notice and an affidavit and must have been necessarily incurred; this is how the landlord's suit costs enter a judgment.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: Judgment is rendered in an NYC Civil Court action between the landlord and a former tenant.
proposed.effect: The clerk taxes the costs, the fees paid to the clerk and the fee for issuing an execution to the sheriff or marshal, and inserts them in the judgment; a transcript includes the prospective county clerk and sheriff fees. Other taxable disbursements are taxed on two days' notice to the adverse party, verified by affidavit, and allowed only if necessarily incurred or performed.
proposed.quote: Costs, together with fees paid to the clerk and the fee for issuing execution to the sheriff or marshal, must be taxed by the clerk forthwith upon rendition of judgment and inserted therein. Upon issuing a transcript the clerk shall include therein the prospective fees of the county clerk and sheriff. Other taxable disbursements shall be taxed by the clerk on two days' notice to be given by the party entitled thereto to the adverse party. The clerk shall also tax costs allowed by an appellate court and shall enter all items of costs and disbursements in the docket book. All disbursements taxable on notice must be verified by affidavit. The clerk must examine all items presented to him for taxation and, before allowing any disbursements, must be satisfied that the items were necessarily incurred or that the services for which they are charged were necessarily performed.

reason: Lists the disbursements a prevailing party (including a self-represented one) recovers in NYC Civil Court: court, sheriff and marshal fees, private process-server cost, witness fees, certified copies, transcript and execution fees.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A party is awarded costs, or prevails having appeared in person, in an NYC Civil Court case over the tenancy.
proposed.effect: Unless a law provides otherwise, it recovers its necessary disbursements: all fees paid to the clerk, sheriff or a marshal, including jury fees, and the reasonable expense of service by a private process server; witnesses' legal fees; fees for certified copies of recorded or filed papers necessarily used at trial; commissioners' reasonable compensation for depositions; prospective charges for filing a transcript and the sheriff's fees for an execution; and other expenses taxable under CPLR 8301. Attorney's fees are not disbursements. Costs and disbursements are recovered only as the judgment awards them; none goes on the final account before judgment (NY:RPL-234-a).
proposed.quote: Except where the contrary is specifically provided by law, a party to whom costs are awarded, or a prevailing party who has appeared in person, shall be allowed his necessary disbursements as follows: (a) All fees paid to the clerk, the sheriff or a marshal, including jury fees, and the reasonable expense of serving process where service is made by other than the sheriff or a marshal. (b) The legal fees of witnesses. (c) The legal fees paid for a certified copy of a deposition or other paper recorded or filed in any public office, necessarily used or obtained for use on the trial. (d) The reasonable compensation of commissioners for taking depositions. (e) Prospective charges for filing a transcript with the county clerk and the sheriff's fees for receiving and returning an execution. (f) Such other reasonable and necessary expenses as are taxable pursuant to the provisions of CPLR § 8301.

reason: If the tenant does not return a CPLR 312-a mail-service acknowledgment within 30 days, the landlord's cost of serving another way is taxed against the tenant; changes the cost of the mail-service route.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord serves a former tenant by mail under CPLR 312-a in NYC Civil Court and the signed acknowledgment is not returned within 30 days after the tenant receives the papers.
proposed.effect: The reasonable expense of serving by another method is taxed by the court as a disbursement payable to the landlord if the landlord is awarded costs.
proposed.quote: In any action where service of process is made by mail pursuant to CPLR 312-a, and where the signed acknowledgement of receipt is not returned within thirty (30) days after receipt of the documents mailed pursuant to that section, the reasonable expense of serving process by an alternative method shall be taxed by the court as a disbursement, payable to the party serving process, if that party is awarded costs in the action or proceeding.

reason: The clerk's taxation of costs can be reviewed only on motion within ten days; otherwise it cannot be challenged on appeal. A deadline for contesting the costs in a judgment.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A party disputes the costs or disbursements the clerk taxed into an NYC Civil Court judgment over the tenancy.
proposed.effect: It moves for review within ten days on two days' notice; the court strikes items wrongly included or adds items wrongly omitted and credits a disallowed sum against any execution. Without that motion the taxation cannot be questioned on appeal.
proposed.quote: Within ten days the clerk's taxation may be reviewed by the court upon two days' notice. The order must disallow any items wrongfully included in the judgment or add any items wrongfully omitted therefrom, and direct that any sum so disallowed be credited upon any execution or other mandate issued to enforce the judgment. Unless a motion for review of the taxation is made, the clerk's taxation cannot be questioned on appeal.

reason: Costs on appeal from the Civil Court; appellate practice, outside the settlement and collection chain.

Sets the NYC Civil Court fees the landlord pays to sue and enforce (summons or first paper $45, jury $70, satisfaction $6, notice of petition $45) and that the $95 consumer-credit surcharge does not apply to a lease balance; an input to the pursue-or-write-off cost and a recoverable disbursement.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A party files in NYC Civil Court in a case over the tenancy.
proposed.effect: Fees, prepaid: issuing a summons or attachment, or filing the summons with proof of service or the first paper in the county, $45 (once); notice of trial $40; entry of judgment on confession $45 unless a summons fee was paid; notice of appeal $30; satisfaction of judgment or certificate $6; jury demand $70, paid by the party demanding; exemplification $15; certified copy $6; notice of petition in a summary proceeding $45; other matters, the Supreme Court fee (not the CPLR 8020(a) motion fee or 8020(d) settlement or discontinuance fee). The added $95 fee on filing the first paper, or on filing a judgment, in an action arising from a consumer credit transaction (CPLR 105(f)) does not apply to a lease balance (NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit). Fees paid are recoverable as disbursements only through the judgment (NY:CCA-1908-disbursements).
proposed.quote: There shall be paid to the clerk the following sums as court fees in an action: (a) Upon issuance of a summons, order of arrest or attachment, or requisition or warrant of seizure by the clerk, together with copies thereof, forty-five dollars. (b) Upon filing summons with proof of service thereof, or upon filing of the first paper in that county in any action or proceeding, forty-five dollars, unless there has been paid in that county a fee of forty-five dollars pursuant to subdivision (a) of this section. (b-1) Upon filing the first paper in an action or proceeding arising out of a consumer credit transaction as defined in subdivision (f) of section one hundred five of the civil practice law and rules, an additional ninety-five dollars. (c) Upon filing an infant's compromise, where no summons was filed, forty dollars. (d) On filing a notice of trial, forty dollars. (e) For entry of judgment upon confession, forty-five dollars, unless there has been paid a fee pursuant to subdivision (a) or subdivision (b) hereof. (f) On filing notice of appeal, thirty dollars. (g) For issuing a satisfaction of judgment, or a certificate regarding the judgment, six dollars. (h) Upon demand for a trial by jury, seventy dollars; to be paid by the party demanding the jury, at the time of demand. (i) For exemplification of any paper filed, fifteen dollars. (j) For certifying a copy of a paper on file in the clerk's office, six dollars. (k) For issuing a notice of petition, or an order to show cause in lieu thereof, in a summary proceeding to recover possession of real property, forty-five dollars. (l) For issuing a petition for change of name, sixty-five dollars. (m) For any other matter, not provided for above, for which there would be a fee payable in the supreme court of a county within the city of New York, the same fee; except that this subdivision shall not apply to the fees required to be paid in supreme court (i) upon the filing of a motion or cross-motion pursuant to subdivision (a) of section 8020 of the civil practice law and rules, and (ii) upon the filing of a stipulation of settlement or a voluntary discontinuance pursuant to subdivision (d) of such section. (n) Upon the filing of a judgment by a plaintiff on or after September first, two thousand ten in an action or proceeding arising out of a consumer credit transaction as defined in subdivision (f) of section one hundred five of the civil practice law and rules, ninety-five dollars, provided such action or proceeding was commenced prior to such date and no additional fee was paid therein pursuant to subdivision (b-1) of this section. All fees shall be prepaid before the service shall be performed.

reason: Sets Civil Court witness fees by reference to Supreme Court witness fees (CPLR 8001, decided there); their recovery is the CCA 1908(b) disbursement. It adds no step or amount of its own.
Caps the NYC Civil Court's money jurisdiction at $50,000; a larger balance or deposit claim goes to Supreme Court. Decides the forum for the suit.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord sues a former tenant for a balance, or the tenant sues for the deposit or damages.
proposed.effect: Branch (a): the amount sought is $50,000 or less: the NYC Civil Court has jurisdiction (small claims up to $10,000: NY:CCA-1801-tenant-claim; commercial claims: NY:CCA-1801-A(a)-eligibility). Branch (b): more than $50,000: the claim goes to the Supreme Court, unless it exceeds the limit only because several claims each within the limit are joined (NY:CCA-211-joinder) or it is a counterclaim (NY:CCA-208-counterclaims).
proposed.quote: The court shall have jurisdiction of actions and proceedings for the recovery of money, actions and proceedings for the recovery of chattels and actions and proceedings for the foreclosure of liens on personal property where the amount sought to be recovered or the value of the property does not exceed $50,000.

reason: In an NYC summary proceeding the court renders judgment for rent due without regard to amount; this fixes what a nonpayment proceeding that preceded the move-out may already have awarded, which the final account credits and does not re-claim.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A summary proceeding to recover possession of an NYC unit, or to remove the tenant, preceded or caused the move-out.
proposed.effect: The Civil Court may render judgment for rent due in the proceeding without regard to amount. Rent awarded there is carried on the final account as a judgment, credited with any payment, and not claimed again; amounts not awarded are pursued by separate action (NY:RPAPL-749(3)-after-proceeding).
proposed.quote: The court shall have jurisdiction over summary proceedings to recover possession of real property located within the city of New York, to remove tenants therefrom, and to render judgment for rent due without regard to amount,

reason: Gives the Civil Court interpleader jurisdiction up to $50,000; the route by which a landlord facing competing claims to a refund (co-tenants, an estate, a trustee) pays it into court.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: Two or more persons make conflicting claims to the deposit refund (for example co-tenants who disagree, a relative and an estate fiduciary), and the amount is $50,000 or less.
proposed.effect: The landlord may bring interpleader in the NYC Civil Court under the CPLR (NY:CPLR-1006-interpleader).
proposed.quote: The court shall have jurisdiction of an action of interpleader and defensive interpleader as defined and governed by the CPLR, provided that the amount in controversy or the value of the property involved does not exceed $50,000.

reason: Where the Chief Administrator has ordered it for the county, a Civil Court money action of $10,000 or less per claim (not small claims) is heard by an arbitration panel; this changes how the landlord's small balance suit is tried.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord's balance action (or the tenant's deposit action) is a civil action for money only in the regular part of the NYC Civil Court, in a county where the Chief Administrator has ordered the arbitration program, seeking $10,000 or less per cause of action exclusive of costs and interest.
proposed.effect: The action is heard and decided by a panel of arbitrators under the court's rules. Actions begun in the small claims part and not transferred are not included. Awards under CPLR article 75 within the court's jurisdiction are confirmed in the Civil Court.
proposed.quote: (b) Proceedings on award under CPLR article 75. Where a controversy has been duly arbitrated and an award made therein is for relief which is within the court's jurisdiction, the court shall have jurisdiction of proceedings under CPLR §§ 7510 through 7514, relating to judicial recognition of such awards, which provisions shall be applicable thereto. (c) Arbitration distinct from CPLR article 75. The rules may provide systems of arbitration and conciliation of claims within the court's jurisdiction without reference to CPLR article 75. Where the chief administrator of the courts has provided by rule for an alternative method of dispute resolution by arbitration and has established by order this arbitration program in any county in this court, applicable in each such county to civil actions for a sum of money only, except those commenced in small claims parts and not subsequently transferred to a regular part of court, that on or after the effective date of such order are noticed for trial or commenced in this court, all such actions shall be heard and decided by a panel of arbitrators where the recovery sought for each cause of action is ten thousand dollars or less, exclusive of costs and interest.

reason: In NYC Civil Court a counterclaim for money is heard without regard to amount; the tenant's deposit counterclaim, or the landlord's balance counterclaim to a tenant's regular-part suit, is not capped at $50,000.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: A party sued in the NYC Civil Court regular part over the tenancy counterclaims for money.
proposed.effect: The court has jurisdiction of a counterclaim within its jurisdiction if sued separately, and of any counterclaim for money only without regard to amount. (Small claims limits counterclaims to its own limit: NY:CCA-1805-small-claims-remedies.)
proposed.quote: The court shall have jurisdiction of counterclaims as follows: (a) Of any counterclaim the subject matter of which would be within the jurisdiction of the court if sued upon separately. (b) Of any counterclaim for money only, without regard to amount.

reason: Allows an order of attachment out of the NYC Civil Court wherever Supreme Court could issue one, and limits injunctions and receivers; a pre-judgment option against a tenant leaving the state or hiding assets.

proposed.instrument: New York City Civil Court Act
proposed.condition: The landlord sues a former tenant in the NYC Civil Court and seeks a remedy before judgment.
